title: origin
definition: The default conventional name that Git assigns to the remote repository that a project was cloned from.
simpleExplanation: 'Origin' is not a magic keyword, it is literally just a nickname. Instead of typing `git push https://github.com/facebook/react.git main` 50 times a day, Git saves that URL in its address book under the nickname 'origin'. You type `git push origin main` instead.
realWorldExample: When you clone a repository, Git automatically sets up the 'origin' remote for you behind the scenes.

basic: Do you HAVE to use the word 'origin'?
intermediate: If you start a project with `git init` instead of `git clone`, does 'origin' exist?

answers.question: Have to use it?
answers.answer: No. You can name your remote 'banana' if you want (`git push banana main`). However, 'origin' is a universal industry standard, and changing it will confuse your coworkers.

answers.question: Does it exist?
answers.answer: No. `git init` creates a purely local repo. You must manually add the remote by typing `git remote add origin <URL>`.

terminalOutput:
# Check where 'origin' actually points to
$ git remote -v
# Output:
# origin  https://github.com/user/repo.git (fetch)
# origin  https://github.com/user/repo.git (push)

# You can change the URL that 'origin' points to!
$ git remote set-url origin https://github.com/user/NEW-repo.git
